name: Panare trade Spanish / Trade Spanish of the Piñaguero Panare
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 2 other works consulted do not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Riley, Carroll L. 1952. Trade Spanish of the Piñaguero Panare. Studies in Linguistics 10(1): 6-11.
catalog_locator: p. 9, §3 'Phonology' (archive.org issue scan = leaf 10); accent marking in the utterances pp. 7-8
catalog_quote: With the exception of a few of the Panare words, the trade language has been phonemically adapted to the local Spanish. Certain native words in the trade jargon seem to be standardized. ... The following native words were found to be used by both Venezuelans and Panare in trading: tewá: 'basket' tó: 'manioc squeezer'. (The Panare pronounce this, [tóʔ]) kamičá: 'cloth' or 'clothing' (perhaps from Spanish 'camisa'). yará: 'murroquoy' (a land tortoise). nyá: 'let's go, goodby'. (This, in Panare, is [ŋá].) In paká 'vaca' and kabayšú 'caballo', the accent has shifted to the last syllable, the common accentuation of Panare words. This accent shift does not occur in the clearly Spanish words of the trade language and, in fact, the Panare consider paká and kabayšú as native in origin. The consonant š of kabayšú is not found in the modern Venezuelan pronunciation of this word (kabáyo). ... In the Spanish word káro the first vowel is lengthened to denote emphasis, thus [ka·ro]. This is also a Venezuelan practice. It appears in a number of words and phrases; in each case the rhetorical length occurs on the stressed syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Words of Spanish origin keep the stress of the local Venezuelan Spanish word (i.e. lexically given Spanish stress, mostly penultimate in the gerund-based verb forms and disyllables of the texts: sabyéndo, sérka, péro, káro); the few words of Panare origin, and the two Spanish loans the Panare treat as native (paká, kabayšú), are stressed on the final syllable, which Riley calls the common accentuation of Panare words. No independent stress rule for the pidgin is formulated beyond 'phonemically adapted to the local Spanish'.
new_statements.exceptions: paká 'vaca' and kabayšú 'caballo': Spanish-origin words whose accent has shifted to the final syllable (Panare pattern) because the Panare regard them as native words; the shift 'does not occur in the clearly Spanish words'. The standardized native trade words (tewá 'basket', tó 'manioc squeezer', kamičá 'cloth', yará 'land tortoise', nyá 'let's go, goodbye') all carry final accent.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level. Statement made in the phonology section of a 6-page sketch of a trade jargon recorded in the field in winter 1950-51; the author says the paper 'cannot claim to present a thorough analysis of the dialect'. Accent is marked with an acute in the cited utterances (pp. 7-8), not discussed as contrastive. Emphatic vowel lengthening ('rhetorical length') is said to fall on the stressed syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Riley describes the trade jargon of the Piñaguero district (San Félix river valley), Northern Panare; footnote 1 says the nearby Pinal group used a similar trade Spanish and that all Northern Panare reportedly used the same dialect in trade. Substrate = Panare/Eñepa (Cariban), Glottolog pana1307; lexifier = local Venezuelan Spanish of interior Bolívar. Data are from one field season (1950-51); the variety is presumably no longer in use and has no later documentation.
